Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
I feel like an object, not like a person
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.explanation: 'Noticing Weapons' is a poor fit for the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is evidence of weapon-related assault or generalized violence cues; the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal abuse and nonspecific danger rather than weapon-focused threat monitoring, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma context.

'Inaction Guilt' is clinically questionable in this context because it implies self-blame for not doing more to stop the abuse, which is less coherent with an ongoing coercive partner-abuse formulation than appraisals centered on shame, powerlessness, betrayal, or worthlessness. It is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it stands out as weakly aligned with the trauma narrative and node pattern.

vignette:
Minh was forty-eight when it happened, though he sometimes felt as though the years before and after had been erased and only that night remained in fragments. He had been with Lina for two years, and he had learned to read the tilt of her jaw, the way her voice would go flat just before she struck. But that evening he had come home late from the office-an audit file had taken longer than expected, and he was tired, so tired that the usual vigilance slipped. She was waiting in the kitchen. The first blow caught him across the cheekbone, and then she was on him, her fists and knees finding his ribs, his thighs, his back. He remembered a white light, the smell of cooking oil, the sound of her breathing. There was a moment when he tried to push her away, and she laughed. Then nothing. A gap. The next thing he knew, he was on the floor, his shirt torn, and she was gone. He never pressed charges. He told himself it was a one-time thing, that he had provoked her, that he was a man and should be able to handle it. But when he looked in the mirror that night he did not see a person; he saw an object, something that had been used and discarded.

The memory did not stay in that night. It arrived in pieces-a flash of her hand, the cold tile against his cheek-without warning, often when he was alone and least expecting it. He would be sitting at his desk at the Revenue Department, reviewing a return, and suddenly the image would push through, and his heart would hammer, and he would have to excuse himself to the restroom. There were long stretches when he could not recall the event at all, not because he was avoiding it, but because the memory simply would not come together; whole minutes were missing, as if someone had cut out a section of film. He would try to reconstruct the sequence, but all he found were gaps, and the effort left him hollow.

What frightened him most, though, was the growing sense that danger had not ended. He began to feel unsafe standing in open rooms; he needed his back against a wall, needed to see every door and every window. At work, he chose a desk in the corner and always sat facing the entrance. He caught himself looking behind him as he walked down the hall, and sometimes he spun around for no reason, certain someone was following. His wife, Thanh, noticed. She asked why he flinched whenever she entered a room quietly. He said it was nothing, but he stopped coming out of the bedroom until he could hear her voice first. At home, he felt most secure with his back to the headboard, scanning the doorway. The false alarms came daily: a car backfiring, a dropped file, a sudden change in a taxpayer's tone-each time his body braced as if for impact. His chest would tighten, and he would be drenched in sweat before he could reason his way back to calm.

The exhaustion made everything worse. Tiredness became a trigger in itself; if he felt fatigue settling in, he knew the fragments would come more easily, and so he began to avoid rest. He stayed up late, working through spreadsheets, because sleep felt like surrender. He also avoided any situation that felt unpredictable-changing his route to work so that he never encountered a surprise, declining dinner invitations because he could not control the seating arrangement. His supervisor noticed that Minh had stopped taking on new audits, and Thanh grew quiet, unsure how to reach him. He had come to believe that nothing good could happen anymore; the world had shown him what it was, and he was merely moving through it, a shell.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning in the office when an intern tapped him on the shoulder from behind. Minh spun around and shoved the young man against a filing cabinet before he knew what he was doing. The intern was shaken, and Minh was asked to take leave. That afternoon, sitting alone in his car, he thought of Lina, of the betrayal, of the feeling that he had been broken and there was nothing left. He called a number Thanh had left on the fridge months ago. He did not know if he could be fixed, but he could not keep living like this-back against the wall, waiting for a blow that never came.
